goalAndTeaching.goal: Complete one evidence-based row of the Australia–Canada chart, then use the film as a film source for Questions 9–14 and Assignment 4.2.
goalAndTeaching.essentialQuestion: How can we compare child-removal policies while keeping each source and experience distinct?
headings: 1. Start with people and precise names
2. Compare a policy, not two interchangeable stories
3. Read the film as a film
goalAndTeaching.firstTeachingExcerpt: The Theme 4 booklet introduces the terminology discussion by Summer May Finlay, a Yorta Yorta woman. Question 7 asks why acronyms can be disrespectful when naming a person. Use a person’s or Nation’s own preferred name when known; “Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples” refers to distinct peoples in Australia. In Canada, First Nations, Inuit and Métis are distinct peoples. A convenient collective label never replaces a person’s identity.

workedResponse.title: Worked chart row: destinations after removal
workedResponse.directions: The assigned chart asks where removed children went in Australia and Canada. Write one short, sourced entry for each country, then state the comparison without equating the institutions.

evidence.text: Removed Aboriginal children were brought up in institutions or fostered into white families.
Children from First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities attended residential schools, often far from home.

reasoning: Locate the exact chart category: destination after removal. Do not answer with a cause or an impact.
Give the Australian destination from Source A and the Canadian destination from Source B.
Name the shared action of separation, then name the institutional difference. Neither source proves that all children followed the same route.
workedResponse.response: Australia: the fact sheet describes children placed in institutions or with white foster families. Canada: the NCTR describes children sent to residential schools, often far from their communities. Both involved separation from family, but the destinations and systems described by these sources are not identical. (Sources A–B.)

supportedControl.wrongFeedback: That collapses the systems and claims “every child” without evidence. The sources name different destinations and do not give one duration for all children.
supportedControl.correctFeedback: This note addresses losses in each country and identifies which source supports each detail. It leaves individual experiences open.

independentTasks.title: Repair a conflated comparison
independentTasks.task: After checking the choice above, rewrite this sentence with one fact from each source: “Australia and Canada used the same schools and every child lost exactly the same things.” Save your first version, compare it with the criteria, then revise if needed.
independentTasks.criteria: A strong repair names a documented Australian placement and a documented Canadian placement; states one shared policy effect without claiming identical institutions or experiences; and attributes the facts to Sources A and B. The criteria unlock after your first save.

differsFrom.evidence: The worked row supplies destinations; this repair adds an evidence-bounded claim about effects.
differsFrom.example: Writes and revises a sentence rather than selecting an option.

independentTasks.criteria: A strong response identifies an assimilation rationale in each source, names who the source describes, distinguishes Australian removal policy from Canadian residential schooling, and states a specific source limit rather than inventing a motive for an individual official. differsFrom.evidence: Uses the rationale row, not the worked destinations or supported loss row.
